source.title: Fail-Closed Alignment for Large Language Models
source.authors: Zachary Coalson; Beth Sohler; Aiden Gabriel; Sanghyun Hong

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. There is minor garbling in Appendix B.3 (for example, a sentence is interrupted around the reported accuracy drop), but it does not make the main relevant results unusable.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies difference-in-means (DIM) refusal-feature ablation and measures harmful-response rates on instruction-tuned models, directly testing the original removal intervention. It also tests addition and cumulative ablation for directions learned by its own training method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports DIM and RDO feature-ablation results in Table 3, but does not report the Table 3 no-ablation ASR values in the table itself. Figure 3 gives direction-by-direction results graphically; the text states only aggregate thresholds and endpoints, so no individual direction values are extracted. Values cited from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study applies the original DIM directional ablation (Eq. 3, all layers and positions) to four instruction-tuned models and reports harmful-response ASR against the no-attack baseline, which is V1's removal test. It measures jailbreak suppression of the DIM direction's activation, which bears on V3's first clause. It trains models under ablation of refusal directions and measures DIM and RDO ablation ASR and jailbreak ASR afterwards, which bears on V3's second clause and on V7. The multi-direction findings (r15–r18) come from structure the method deliberately trains in, so they do not test V4 for refusal as it arises in models.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also state that standard alignment encodes refusal along a single dominant direction even though other features exist, so suppressing it collapses alignment (fail-open). Their method trains under ablation of all previously found directions to build redundant, causally independent refusal pathways. It gives ≤4% jailbreak ASR and low feature-ablation ASR while preserving utility.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses the original DIM ablation intervention in evaluation, but uses gradient-based RDO rather than DIM to identify directions for its training method. It tests feature removal and added learned directions, not the original paper's full layer-and-position sweep as a reproduction.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with the feature being ablated (DIM versus RDO), the model, the number of training iterations, and whether training uses multi-feature or single-feature ablation. The reported learned-direction activation suppression also varies by attack and direction.

fits_no_version.finding: Refusal directions learned by the fail-closed method in Llama3-8B: three induce refusal when added (CR <10%), jointly ablating all ten leaves 1% ASR, and jailbreaks suppress r1–r5 by only 10–58%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training can be designed so that refusal is mediated redundantly by several independent linear directions, none of which is a single point of failure.

record.problems: The paper gives no no-ablation ASR values alongside Table 3. Individual direction-addition results in Figure 3 are not numerically stated in the text. Some aggregate table values and figure results are reported without uncertainty; the main evaluation selects checkpoints using held-out ASR.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 results for other training baselines' DIM/RDO ablations are omitted because the catalog prioritizes the base DIM results and the study's own progressive-alignment results. Per-attack, per-model Table 1 ASR entries are omitted because the flattened table layout does not reliably support assigning all values; the authors' aggregate text result is recorded in r14. Individual plotted values in Figure 3 are not extracted where the text supplies only aggregate thresholds or ranges.

untested.parts: Adding the base model's DIM direction to harmless prompts to induce refusal; retention of general capabilities after DIM ablation in base models.
No weight-edit or abliterated released models.
No causal test that jailbreaks succeed because of DIM suppression; the evidence is correlational activation measurements.
No analysis of multiple, affine or cone refusal structure in standard models. Multi-direction results are only for deliberately trained models.

missing.what: The 'w/o RDO' variant on Gemma2-2B iteratively ablates DIM directions during training and reaches ASR 0.9, with a 5.5% accuracy drop. This is direct evidence for V3's training-against-DIM-ablation clause and shows a capability cost.

DeepRefusal, a baseline that trains against single DIM direction ablation: DIM-ablation ASR 1.0/16.0/0.0/9.0 and RDO-ablation ASR 2.5/37.5/22.0/6.5 across the four models, plus its jailbreak ASR. Single-direction training leaves residual vulnerability on Llama3-8B and Gemma2-2B.
Base-model RDO ablation ASR: 63.5, 93.0, 93.0 and 44.0, a second single-direction removal measure.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The base-model results (Figure 1, Table 3) are a fairly close replication of the DIM ablation, but they cover only removal. Checkpoints for the trained models were selected on held-out ASR. The multi-direction findings describe engineered models, so they are kept off V4. The two suppression figures for the base DIM direction ('up to 75%' and '43–71%') are inconsistent.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests DIM removal in base instruction-tuned models, but does not test adding the base model's DIM direction to benign prompts, nor whether general capabilities remain intact specifically after that ablation.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration experiment is reported.

The study tests suppression of refusal-direction activations under prompt jailbreaks and robustness after its own ablation-based training. It does not test whether training specifically against a jailbreak's suppression of the original DIM direction adds robustness.
The study examines multiple directions learned by its method, but does not compare affine, cone, and dominant-direction-plus-others descriptions as competing general accounts of refusal.
The study does not separately measure harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or model-variant transfer of a direction is tested.

The study tests its progressive training procedure and selected training configurations, not a broad comparison of how refusal-training histories determine whether a single removable direction exists.
